paper.title: Correcting DFT formation energies towards experimental accuracy using foundational MLIPs and latent-feature delta-learning
paper.file_name: 35_Correcting DFT formation energies towards experimental accuracy using foundational MLIPs and latent-feature delta-learning.pdf
paper.research_summary: The paper introduces thermodynamic stability data for the Materials Cloud three-dimensional crystals database (MC3D) and validates it against other DFT databases. It then improves agreement of DFT formation energies with experimental formation enthalpies by first using zero-shot foundational machine learning interatomic potentials (fMLIPs) trained at the r2SCAN level (PET-OMATPES), reducing mean absolute error (MAE) by >40% relative to GGA without additional DFT calculations. Finally, it trains classical ML models (KRR, RF, GPR) in a delta-learning framework on latent features from PET-OMATPES to further correct formation energies, achieving MAE <50 meV/atom — comparable to experimental uncertainty — while limiting distortion of relative phase stability via regularization.

tasks.task_name_raw: Correcting DFT formation energies towards experimental accuracy
tasks.objective: Improve the agreement of density functional theory (DFT) calculated formation energies with experimental formation enthalpies.
constraints: limit impact on relative phase stability
reduce mean absolute error below 50 meV/atom
input_requirements: foundational MLIP (e.g., PET-OMATPES) trained at r2SCAN level
output_goal: formation energies with MAE <50 meV/atom vs. experiment
stability classifications (e.g., energy above hull) that preserve physically meaningful relative phase ordering

evidence.text: Correcting DFT formation energies towards experimental accuracy using foundational MLIPs and latent-feature delta-learning

Our results validate and extend the established practice of combining PBEsol geometries with meta-GGA energies to the era of foundational MLIPs. Finally, we train classical machine learning models to further correct the formation energies in a delta-learning framework, where we use the information-rich latent features of the foundational MLIP. These models further reduce the mean absolute error below 50 meV/atom, bringing it down to values comparable with the experimental uncertainty itself.
The central contribution of this work is the improvement of formation energy agreement with experiment.

stages.stage_goal: Obtain formation energies from multiple DFT databases (MC3D, OQMD, Materials Project) for cross-validation and baseline comparison.

evidence.text: We then compare the DFT calculated formation energies against experimental formation enthalpies (see Methods for dataset details). This comparison is practically important, as thermodynamic stability is the most widely used descriptor for filtering materials in computational materials science studies [22, 55–60], and it is particularly relevant for MC3D, which focuses on experimentally known compounds and is intended to support experimentalists.

In addition to the comparison with experimental data, the MC3D formation energies are compared against the established high-throughput databases Materials Project [7, 8] and Open Quantum Materials Database [10]. We query the OQMD v1.5 (locally hosted) and MP v2023.11.1, and match structures by their ICSD ID.

stages.stage_goal: Assess the accuracy of formation energies predicted by foundational MLIPs (PET-OMATPES) evaluated on DFT-relaxed geometries, without retraining or structural relaxation.
stage_output: error metrics (MAE, ME, RMSE) vs. experiment

stages.stage_name_raw: Training classical ML models in delta-learning framework
stages.stage_goal: Train classical ML models (KRR, RF, GPR) to predict the residual (delta) between calculated formation energies (PBEsol or zero-shot MLIP) and experimental values, using latent features from PET-OMATPES as input.

evidence.text: We train classical machine learning models to further correct the formation energies in a delta-learning framework, where we use the information-rich latent features of the foundational MLIP.

The three models from the Methods section (Random Forest (RF) [69], Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) [70] with a RBF and Laplacian (LAP) kernel, Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) [71]) are trained on two targets: (i) δ∆HPBEsol_f, the difference between PBEsol formation energies and experiment, and (ii) δ∆HMLIP_f, the difference between zero-shot r2SCAN MLIP formation energies (on top of the PBEsol structures) and experiment.

stages.stage_goal: Evaluate the performance of the ML-corrected formation energies against experimental references and quantify improvements in MAE and impact on relative phase stability (stability flip rate).
stage_input: test set formation energies (PBEsol or MLIP)

evidence.text: These models further reduce the mean absolute error below 50 meV/atom, bringing it down to values comparable with the experimental uncertainty itself.

Fig. 3a shows the test MAE for each model and feature combination across 30 train-test splits; hyperparameters were selected based on the best average cross-validation MAE across all 30 splits, and each bar reports the average test MAE for models trained with that best hyperparameter set, with error bars indicating the standard deviation across splits.

stages.stage_name_raw: Studying regularization impact on accuracy-stability trade-off
stages.stage_goal: Systematically vary regularization strength (α in KRR) to analyze its effect on the trade-off between formation energy prediction accuracy (MAE) and distortion of relative phase stability (stability flip rate).

evidence.text: We now examine how regularization, controlled by the α parameter in KRR, mediates the trade-off between formation energy accuracy and distortion of relative phase stability. Fig. 4a shows this trade-off for KRR models with Laplacian and RBF kernels, each paired with Magpie or LF features.
Based on the trade-off in Fig. 4a and b, we select the KRR-LAP-LF model with α = 0.1.

evidence.text: In this work, we introduce formation energies to the Materials Cloud three-dimensional crystals database [17], a fully reproducible and open-source DFT curated database of three-dimensional inorganic crystal structures with a particular focus on experimentally known compounds. Here, we focus on the versions PBE-v1 and PBEsol-v1 of MC3D.

In addition to the comparison with experimental data, the MC3D formation energies are compared against the established high-throughput databases Materials Project [7, 8] and Open Quantum Materials Database [10]. We query the OQMD v1.5 (locally hosted) and MP v2023.11.1, and match structures by their ICSD ID.

Fig. 2b shows that zero-shot formation energies [62] from the PET-OMATPES model [63, 64]—one of the top-performing models in community benchmarks at the time of publication [65], trained on the OMAT [66] and MATPES [37] datasets at the r2SCAN level—reduce the MAE by more than 40% when evaluated at the DFT (GGA) relaxed geometry.

Fig. 2b shows that zero-shot formation energies [62] from the PET-OMATPES model [63, 64]—one of the top-performing models in community benchmarks at the time of publication [65], trained on the OMAT [66] and MATPES [37] datasets at the r2SCAN level—reduce the MAE by more than 40% when evaluated at the DFT (GGA) relaxed geometry.

We validate the use of PET-OMATPES r2SCAN formation energies as the baseline for δ∆HMLIP_f targets against the Alexandria database (see SI Fig. S9). Since no meta-GGA DFT version of MC3D currently exists, Alexandria serves as the reference and confirms that the MLIP-estimated stability data agrees well with DFT, validating the use of the PET-OMATPES r2SCAN formation energies and energies above hull as the reference for the stability flip rate analysis.
